strengths: Proposes a comprehensive two-stage framework (InsertAnywhere) that successfully combines 4D scene geometry understanding with diffusion-based video generation for realistic video object insertion.

Introduces ROSE++, a novel illumination-aware synthetic dataset for video object insertion, built by inverting the object-removal ROSE dataset and leveraging VLMs to retrieve clean reference object images.
Solves complex physical and geometric challenges in video editing, such as occlusion handling, dynamic scene-flow object propagation, and realistic local lighting/shadow synthesis.

The proposed pipeline demonstrates remarkable qualitative improvements over commercial video generators (Kling, Pika Pro), particularly in preserving scene background, maintaining object fidelity, and correctly rendering occlusions.
Provides a thorough evaluation consisting of both objective metrics (CLIP-I, DINO-I, VBench) and a user study, backed by solid ablation studies for each component.
weaknesses: The framework relies on a highly complex pipeline of multiple heavy pretrained models (e.g., Uni4D components, UniDepth, CoTracker/SEA-RAFT, SAM 2, and single-view 3D reconstruction). The cascading error from any of these upstream modules and its impact on final inference speed/robustness is not thoroughly discussed.

The evaluation on VOIBench (50 videos, 100 test cases) is relatively small, and comparison is primarily restricted to closed-source commercial APIs (Pika, Kling). Incorporating academic video-editing baselines (such as GenProp or InVi) in the main table would strengthen the experimental validation.

The method's performance is highly dependent on the quality of the first-frame image-based inpainting. If the first frame produces artifacts or incorrect lighting, these errors will propagate throughout the video sequence.

strengths: The proposed two-stage framework successfully combines 4D scene geometry understanding with diffusion-based video generation, addressing both accurate spatial placement/occlusion handling and photorealistic appearance/lighting synthesis.

The introduction of the ROSE++ dataset is a clever contribution, creatively inverting an object-removal dataset into an object-insertion dataset by using VLMs and DINO similarity to construct high-quality, clean reference object images.

The method demonstrates significant qualitative and quantitative improvements over state-of-the-art commercial systems (Kling, Pika-Pro) in complex scenarios involving severe occlusions, dynamic camera motions, and ambient lighting changes.
The ablation studies and supplementary materials are comprehensive, proving the necessity of each component (e.g., scene-flow-based propagation, first-frame inpainting, and LoRA fine-tuning).
weaknesses: The 4D mask generation stage is highly complex and relies on a long chain of external models (Uni4D, UniDepthv2, SEA-RAFT, SAM2, and single-view 3D reconstruction). This pipeline-heavy design increases the risk of error propagation and makes the entire system computationally heavy.

The quantitative evaluation lacks comparisons against other academic, open-source video object insertion or video editing baselines (such as VideoAnyDoor, InVi, or GenProp), focusing primarily on closed-source commercial APIs (Kling, Pika-Pro).

There is no discussion on the overall computational footprint, execution time, or inference latency of the proposed pipeline, which is likely substantial given the multi-model reconstruction, interactive user alignment, and a 14B parameter video diffusion model.
The user-guided placement of the 3D point cloud makes the system semi-automatic and restricts its applicability in fully automated, batch-processing workflows.

strengths: The paper addresses a highly practical and relevant problem: Video Object Insertion (VOI) with precise geometric control, occlusion handling, and physical/photometric consistency, which is highly valuable for media editing and advertising.
The overall system design is logical and well-conceived, effectively bridging the gap between explicit 3D/4D spatial reasoning and generative 2D video diffusion models.

The creation of the ROSE++ dataset is a clever workaround to the lack of training data for video object insertion. Converting an object-removal dataset into a supervised insertion triplet dataset using VLM-guided reference image generation is a solid contribution.
The qualitative results on challenging real-world videos demonstrate impressive handling of dynamic occlusions, shadows, and camera movement.
weaknesses: The technical and algorithmic novelty is quite limited. The entire pipeline relies heavily on a sequence of off-the-shelf modules (Uni4D for scene reconstruction, SEA-RAFT for tracking, SAM2 for mask refinement, OmniPaint for first-frame inpainting, and Wan2.1-VACE for video generation). The paper acts more like a system integration paper rather than introducing a fundamental generative or geometric model.

The comparison with baselines is incomplete and somewhat unfair. The paper primarily compares its performance against commercial closed-source models (Pika-Pro and Kling) which are text-to-video or basic image-to-video models and do not support explicit 3D coordinate inputs or 4D masks. A rigorous evaluation should include comparison against academic video editing and insertion baselines that utilize regional/mask controls (e.g., InVi, AnyV2V, GenProp, or VideoAnyDoor).

The pipeline exhibits strong dependencies on the accuracy of the 4D reconstruction (Uni4D) and optical flow (SEA-RAFT). If the input video contains rapid camera motion, low texture, or highly dynamic background elements, these estimation steps can easily fail, causing the entire insertion pipeline to produce misaligned masks. Furthermore, propagating motion using the local flow field (Eq. 2) restricts the method to objects that move strictly with their immediate 3D neighbors, failing for independently moving objects.

There is a potential domain gap in the ROSE++ dataset training. Since the reference images in ROSE++ are VLM-generated based on cropped video objects, they might exhibit specific distribution patterns. At test time, a user might provide arbitrary real-world product images, and the mismatch between VLM-generated training references and real test references is not thoroughly discussed or evaluated.

strengths: Presents a comprehensive framework that successfully addresses two core challenges of video object insertion: precise 3D placement and realistic out-of-mask lighting synthesis (shadows and reflections).

The Optics-Aware Representation Alignment strategy is an elegant solution to teach the model to synthesize effects beyond the spatial mask boundary during training, without requiring extended masks at inference time.
Constructs and open-sources ROSE++, a valuable quadruplet dataset designed specifically for supervising physical lighting interactions in video object insertion.
Strong qualitative and quantitative results against both established research baselines and state-of-the-art commercial tools, supported by user studies.
weaknesses: The pipeline is highly complex and relies on a large stack of external vision models (depth estimation, optical flow, camera pose, TRELLIS for 3D lifting, Uni4D, SAM 2, Omnipaint, and Wan2.1-VACE), which increases the potential for cumulative errors and points of failure.
High computational cost, taking around 8.5 minutes on a B200 GPU to process an 81-frame video, which limits its applicability to real-time or interactive scenarios.

The alignment loss (Eq. 7) forces the fine-mask features to align with the coarser extended-mask features. While the paper notes that object appearance fidelity is largely insensitive to this loss, a more detailed analysis of whether this alignment causes any loss of fine texture details inside the object mask would be beneficial.

strengths: A well-designed, two-stage framework that simultaneously tackles the geometric (placement, occlusion, tracking) and photometric (shadows, reflections) challenges of Video Object Insertion (VOI).

The proposed Optics-Aware Representation Alignment is an elegant and effective solution. It allows mask-conditioned models to learn out-of-mask optical effects (like shadows) during training using an extended mask teacher, without needing extended masks during inference.

The creation and release of the ROSE++ dataset (a supervised dataset for optical effects training) and VOIBench represent valuable, practical contributions to the video editing and computer vision community.

Comprehensive evaluation combining automated metrics (CLIP-I, DINO-I, VBench), targeted ablation studies (e.g., evaluating PSNR specifically within the shadow/optics regions), and thorough user studies.
weaknesses: High computational complexity and inference cost: The pipeline stacks multiple heavy model architectures (Uni4D, TRELLIS, SEA-RAFT, SAM 2, image insertion, and Wan2.1-VACE-14B). Taking ~8.5 minutes on a B200 GPU for a brief video limits its interactive usability and consumer appeal.

Heavy dependency on the image-level insertion model (first-frame anchoring). If the image editing model generates suboptimal perspective, incorrect lighting, or visual artifacts on the first frame, these errors are propagated and locked throughout the remaining frames.

The paper lacks discussion and visual examples of failure cases, such as when the 4D scene reconstruction fails (e.g., in highly dynamic, textureless, or specular environments) or when KNN scene flow tracking drifts.

strengths: The paper presents a complete and well-structured framework that successfully addresses two major pain points in video object insertion: 4D spatial grounding (including occlusions and camera motion) and photorealistic out-of-mask lighting effects (cast shadows and reflections).

The Optics-Aware Representation Alignment strategy is technically sound and highly elegant. By using an extended-mask teacher branch with a stop-gradient during training, it successfully enables mask-conditioned models to generate realistic lighting effects beyond the tight object boundary during inference.

The 4D mask generation pipeline effectively integrates multiple state-of-the-art vision models (Uni4D, TRELLIS, SEA-RAFT, SAM 2) to build a robust, user-friendly 3D placement and temporal propagation module.

The paper contributes valuable assets to the community, including the specialized ROSE++ training dataset, the VOIBench evaluation benchmark, and exhaustive quantitative, qualitative, and user-study comparisons that clearly demonstrate superiority over both academic and commercial baselines.
weaknesses: The framework heavily relies on a cascade of multiple foundation models (depth, flow, segmentation, image-to-3D, etc.). Failure or error accumulation in any of these upstream modules (e.g., inaccurate metric depth or poor 3D reconstruction from TRELLIS) can severely degrade the overall mask generation and video synthesis.

The computational and temporal cost of the pipeline is high, requiring approximately 8.5 minutes on a premium NVIDIA B200 GPU for a short video clip (81 frames). This high latency limits its potential for real-time or interactive editing applications.

While the supplementary material describes how the extended mask is processed to filter noise, the paper could benefit from a more detailed discussion on how robust the frame-differencing and morphological operations are against realistic compression artifacts or subtle lighting/camera noise in non-synthetic source videos.
